# Virginia Department of Health Announces First Measles-Associated Death in 2026

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE — November 20, 2026 Media Contact: Brookie Crawford, brookie.crawford@vdh.virginia.gov

Virginia Department of Health Announces First Measles-Associated Death in 2026

RICHMOND, Va. — The Virginia Department of Health (VDH) is reporting that a young child (0-4 years) who tested positive for measles has died. This death is Virginia’s first measles-associated death in 2026. To protect the family’s privacy, VDH will not provide any further information regarding this death.

Measles can cause serious illness, including pneumonia, brain inflammation, complications during pregnancy, and death. Measles virus can also damage immune cells that help the body protect against viruses and bacteria it has encountered before, causing additional vulnerability to health. Although anyone can become seriously ill, children younger than five years old, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk of complications.

There has been a recent increase in measles activity in some areas of Virginia. VDH urges Virginians to be proactive in protecting themselves and their communities from measles and avoiding future tragedies such as this. The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the best way to prevent and stop the spread of measles. Two doses of the vaccine provide lifetime protection, offering approximately 97% effectiveness at preventing measles.

Virginia residents can check their vaccination records using the VDH record request portal or by calling their healthcare provider. People who develop fever and rash, especially if they have been exposed to measles or are not vaccinated, should contact their healthcare provider. They should call ahead before visiting a clinic or hospital so steps can be taken to prevent exposing others.

VDH’s Measles Dashboard will be next updated Tuesday, November 24 to reflect this information.

There has been some concern about the virus spreading as families and friends gather for Thanksgiving next week and for Christmas and other holidays in December. But experts say most adults do not need a booster shot, though some are good candidates for one. This month the CDC put out new guidance on measles and pregnancy noting an increased risk of miscarriage and babies born with congenital infections, as well as health problems such as pneumonia for pregnant women.

A young child who tested positive for measles has died in Virginia, health officials announced on Friday, marking the first measles-associated death in the state this year.
The child was between the ages of 0 and 4, according to the Virginia Department of Health.
The majority of measles cases in 2026 have been confirmed among children and teenagers aged 19 and younger, according to the CDC.
The Virginia Department of Health did not release an exact age but said the child was between the ages of 0 and 4. The department said it is not releasing any further information on the death to protect the family's privacy. "There has been a recent increase in measles activity in some areas of Virginia," the department said in a news release on Friday.
